ABSTRACT
Understanding the components composition characteristics of human milk is conductive for the development of
infant formulas. The total fatty acids composition and the stereo-distribution of fatty acids in human milk tri-
glycerides (TGs) from three regions (Zhengzhou, Wuhan and Harbin) of China were analyzed. The total and
intrapositional fatty acids composition of human milk TGs showed signi ﬁcant di ﬀerences among three regions.
Zhengzhou, Harbin and Wuhan human milk possessed highest levels of medium-chain fatty acids (MCFA,
6.36 ± 1.46%), short-chain fatty acids (SCFA, 0.10 ± 0.03%) and monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA,
34.61 ± 0.45%), and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA, 30.34 ± 0.33%), respectively. The preference dis-
tribution of fatty acids in human milk TGs was hardly a ﬀected by regions, for the relative conservative inter-
positional levels of each fatty acids in three regions. Not only the speci ﬁc distribution of sn-2 position, but the
esteriﬁcation of fatty acids in sn-1 and sn-3 positions also had preference. SCFA and MCFA were mainly esteri ﬁed
at sn-3 position, but LCSFA most unlikely distributed at the sn-3 position. The preference esteri ﬁcation of MUFA
were sn-1, sn-3 > sn-2, and PUFA were sn-3 > sn-1 > sn-2. Therefore, the optimization of infant formulas not
only needs considering total fatty acid composition of TGs but requires thinking over the stereo-distribution of
fatty acids.
1. Introduction
Human milk was considered as gold standards for infants ’ nutrition,
in which lipids (3 –5%) was one of the main nutritional components.
Over 98% of human milk lipids was accounted by TGs ( Koletzko, 2016).
Fatty acid composition and distribution in human milk are very dis-
tinctive, which is the best reference for designing infant formulas.
Palmitic acid, oleic acid and linoleic acid were the most abundant fatty
acids in human milk ( Wang et al., 2020). It was found that the levels of
linoleic acid in China were far higher than other countries ( Qi et al.,
2018). It was also reported that in Chinese human milk, oleic –palmi-
tic–linoleic (OPL) was more abundant than oleic –palmitic–oleic (OPO),
which was contrary to most European countries ( Sun et al., 2018; Tu,
Ma, Bai, & Du, 2017 ). Zhang et al. (2019) also proved that in Chinese
human milk, O-P-L representing the main TG, followed by O-P-O and O-
L-L. The high levels of linoleic acid and OPL in Chinese human milk
were related to the intake of vegetable oil, especially soybean oil ( Qi
et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020). Fatty acids pro ﬁles of human milk in
diﬀerent regions was very di ﬀerent, mainly because the di ﬀerent
dietary habit ( Deng et al., 2013). For example, compared with inland
area, river/lake and coastal areas possessed higher levels of PUFA
(Claumarchirant et al., 2016). Deng et al. (2013) reported that SFA in
breast milk was positively correlated with the maternal intake of meat.
Therefore, the vast area of China leading to massive di ﬀerences in diet
in di ﬀerent regions, may impact the fatty acids composition in human
milk. It is very important to de ﬁnite the concentration ﬂuctuation of
each fatty acid.
Not only the fatty acids composition, but the distribution of fatty
acids in TGs also have physiological function for infants. In human
milk, the distribution of fatty acids is not random, and the speci ﬁc

distribution of palmitic acid have paid much attention. Above 70% of
palmitic acid esteri ﬁed in sn-2 position in human milk TGs, and sn-1/3
positions were usually occupied by unsaturated fatty acids ( Qi et al.,
2018; Wu et al., 2019). The main regioisomers of OPO and OPL, which
were the most two abundant TGs in human milk, were proved as 1,3-
dioleoyl-2-palmitoylglycerol ( rac-OPO) and 1-oleoyl-2-palmitoyl-3-li-
noleoylglycerol ( rac-OPL) ( Kallio, Nylund, Bostrom, & Yang, 2017). A
high sn-2 position palmitic acid diet was bene ﬁcial for fat and calcium
absorption, which further improved bone strength, reduced crying and
increased fecal bi ﬁdobacterial ( Lo’pez-Lo’pez et al., 2001; Miles &
Calder, 2017 ). Wang, Liu, Liu, Sun, and Li (2019) reported that the
intake of OPO can promote the absorption of fat and calcium and the
growth of bene ﬁcial bacteria, including Biﬁdobacteriaceae and Lacto-
bacillaceae. However, infants had a di ﬀerent digestion and absorption
process with adults. Fat intake per kilogram bodyweight in infants was
3–5 folds higher compared to adults, because fat in infants not only for
providing energy but for good growth. It was found that gastric lipase
can hydrolysis 1.7 –2.5 times higher of TGs from human milk than that
from infant formulas, which was mainly related to the di ﬀerent TGs
structure ( Billeaud et al., 2018 ). Gastric lipase has a strong sn-3 ste-
reoselectivity, mainly release medium and long chain fatty acids in
stomach ( Roman et al., 2007). The long chain fatty acids released by
gastric lipase play an important role in triggering the activity of pan-
creatic lipase and essential for TG totally digestion ( Bernbäck,
Bläckberg, & Hernell, 1990). So, in human milk, not only the total and
sn-2 fatty acids, but the speci ﬁc distribution of sn-1 and sn-3 fatty acids
may also have important physiological function for infants. However,
most of studies only focused on total pro ﬁle and regio-distribution of
fatty acids ( Qi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020 ). But the sn-3 position
speciﬁc distribution or the di ﬀerences between sn-1 and sn-3
position of
fatty acids in human milk TGs received little attention. Therefore, the
informations about the stereo-distribution, including intrapositional
and interpositional compositions of fatty acids in human milk TGs
should also be researched.
The purposes of this paper were to understand the total fatty acids
composition and fatty acids stereo-distribution (intrapositional and
interpositional compositions of fatty acids) in human milk TGs. To ex-
plore the impact of di ﬀerent geographical regions ( Fig. 1), human milk
from Zhengzhou (located in the Yellow River drainage aeras, and prefer
pasta food), Wuhan (located in the Yangtze River drainage areas, and
with high intake of fresh-water food) and Harbin (located in Northeast
China, where belongs to the mid-temperate continental monsoon cli-
mate, and with rice as staple food) were analyzed.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Reagents and standards samples
The standards of fatty acid methyl esters (FAME, C4:0-C22:6) mix
(n = 37), porcine pancreatic lipase, L-a-phosphatidylcholine and L-a-
lysophosphatidylcholine were purchased from Sigma Aldrich Chemical
Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Triolein, 2-monoolein, 1,2-diolein 2-
monoolein were purchased from Larodan Fine Chemicals (Malmö,
Sweden). Thin-layer chromatography (TLC, 0.5 mm, 10 cm × 20 cm),
coated with silica gel G and not containing dichloro ﬂuorescein, were
purchased from Anhui Liangchen Silicon Material Co. Ltd. (Anhui,
China). All other solvents were analytical grade and purchased from
Sinopharm Chemical Reagent (Shanghai, China).
2.2. Human milk samples
Human milk was collected before breastfeeding at 9:0 –11:0 in the
morning and from 96 to 180 days after delivery. Volunteer mothers
(25–35 years old) from the hospitals in three provincial capital
Zhengzhou (Zhengzhou Zhenggong Hospital, n = 30), Wuhan
(Zhoutoujie Health Service Center, Hanyang District, n = 30) and
Harbin (Harbin Gongnong Community Health Service Center, n = 30),
diﬀerence regions in China, respectively, all received detailed in-
formation about the study and provided written informed consent.
Mothers were all long-term residents with typical eating habits and
physically healthy by self-evaluation, not smoke, not drink alcohol and
had given birth to physically health infants. Mothers were instructed to
wash their hands carefully with soap and water before expressing of
their milk from one breast by breast pump into sterile hard plastic
containers. The collection human milk sample information was regis-
tered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT03675204). All The samples were
kept frozen at −20 °C until delivery to the laboratory, then dispensed
and stored at −80 °C for subsequent analysis. And all samples were
analyzed separately.
2.3. Determination of fat content
Determination of fat content in human milk by human milk com-
ponent analyzer (Miris HMA, Sweden).
2.4. Extraction lipids from human milk
Lipids fraction from human milk were extracted using Folch pro-
cedure ( Folch et al., 1957). Brie ﬂy, 10 mL human milk was added to
40 mL chloroform/methanol (2/1, v/v), mixed thoroughly ice bath for
30 min and then centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 5 min. The chloroform
layers were collected and the water layers were re-extracted with
2 × 20 mL chloroform: methanol (2/1, v/v). The organic phases were
evaporated by rotary vacuum evaporator. The obtained total lipids
were stored at −20 °C for further analysis.
2.5. Analysis of total and stereo-distribution of fatty acids in human milk
TGs
2.5.1. Fatty acids composition of TGs
TGs were separated from other lipids class by TLC with a solvent
system of hexane/diethyl ether/acetic acid (80/20/1, v/v/v), and the
develop time were about 40 min. All TLC were visualized with 2,7-di-
chloroﬂuorescein spray (0.1% in ethanol). The band corresponding to
TGs was scraped o ﬀ and extracted with diethyl ether. Then 10 mg milk
TGs was methylated and analyzed by gas chromatography as described
in the Section 2.5.4 .
2.5.2. Pancreatic lipase hydrolysis
Sn-2 fatty acids composition was performed according to ( Luddy

et al., 1964) with slight modi ﬁcations. Brie ﬂy, 30 mg milk TGs, ob-
tained from 2.4, were mixed with 0.6 mL of Tris bu ﬀer (1 M; pH 8),
0.06 mL of aqueous CaCl2 solution (22%), 0.15 mL of bile salts (0.1%)
and 6 mg of pancreatic lipase. The mixture was reacted in a shaking
bath with 160 rpm, at 45 °C for 10 min and then stopped by adding
0.2 mL HCl (6 M) followed by 0.2 mL diethyl ether. The diethyl ether
was collected, and separated on a thin-layer chromatography (TLC)
with a developing solvent system comprising hexane/diethyl ether/
acetic acid (50/50/1, v/v/v), and the develop time were about 40 min.
All TLC were visualized with 2,7-dichloro ﬂuorescein spray (0.1% in
ethanol). The band corresponding to sn-2 monoglycerides was scraped
oﬀ and then methylated and analyzed by gas chromatography as de-
scribed in the Section 2.5.4 .
2.5.3. Grignard hydrolysis
Analysis of the fatty acids composition of sn-1 position was per-
formed according to ( Blasi et al., 2008 ). In brief, milk TGs (40 mg),
obtained from Section 2.4, were degradation using 170 μL ethyl mag-
nesium bromide (3 M). Sn-1,2(2,3)-DAG were isolated by TLC with
boric acid impregnated silica gel using hexane/diethyl ether (1/1, v/v)
as developing solvent. The chemical synthesis of sn-1,2(2,3)-phospha-
tidylcholine ( sn-1,2(2,3)-PC) was performed by use 0.65 mL of a mix-
ture of chloroform/ pyridine/ phosphorous oxychloride (9.5/9.5/1, v/
v/v) for 1 h at 4 °C and 1 h at 25 °C, respectively. The solution was then
added with 200 mg choline chloride reaction in a shaking bath with
160 rpm, at 30 °C for 10 h and then for 30 min more after addition of
20 μL of water. Sn-1-lysophosphatidylcholines ( sn-1-LPC) were ob-
tained by hydrolysis of sn-1,2(2,3)-PC with1 mg of phospholipase A2
(≥600 U/mg, dissolved in 0.5 mL Tris bu ﬀer solution at pH 8.9 con-
taining 4 mM calcium chloride), and reacted in a shaking bath with
160 rpm, at 32 °C for 4 h. Finally, sn-1-LPC were isolated by TLC using
the mixture chloroform/methanol/water (65/25/4, v/v/v), and iden-
tiﬁed using L-a-lysophosphatidylcholine as standard reference com-
pounds. All TLC were visualized with 2,7-dichloro ﬂuorescein spray
(0.1% in ethanol). The fatty acid composition of sn-1-LPC was methy-
lated and analyzed by gas chromatography as described in the Section
2.5.4.
The fatty acids composition of sn-3 position (A3) was obtained
starting from the % fatty acids composition of total TG (At), applying
the following formula: A3 = 3 × At-A1-A2, where A3 = % intraposi-
tional composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in sn-3 position, At = % total
composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in the three sn positions of TGs,
A1 = % intrapositional composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in sn-1
position,
A2 = % intrapositional composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in
sn-2 position.
The percentage interpositional distributions, which showed the
percentage distribution of each fatty acids in three sites of the glycerol
backbone, were obtained by normalizing to 100 the percentage in-
trapositional fatty acids compositions of the sn-1 (A1), sn-2 (A2) and sn-
3 (A3) positions of each fatty acid composition of TGs, applying the
following equation ( sn-1 interpositional fatty acids composition as ex-
ample): Ae1 = A1/(3 × At) × 100%, where Ae1 = % interpositional
composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in sn-1 position, A1 = % in-
trapositional composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in sn-1 position,
At = % total composition of fatty acids esteri ﬁed in the three sn posi-
tions of TGs.
2.5.4. Gas chromatography analysis
FAMEs were prepared as follows: fat samples were ﬁrst reacted with
0.5 M NaOH-MeOH, at 100 °C for 5 min. Then the mixture were reacted
with 14% boron tri ﬂuoride (dissolved in methanol) at 100 °C for
30 min. FAMEs were extracted with 100 μL n-hexane, then 1 μL FAMEs
injected in a gas chromatograph (GC) (Thermo-Fisher Scienti ﬁc,
Waltham, MA, USA) equipped with a ﬂame ionization detector, and a
capillary column (Supelco SP 2560, 100 m × 0.25 mm × 0.2 μm,
Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The oven temperature was
maintained at 100 °C for 5 min and then increased at 4 °C/min to
240 °C. The temperature of the injector and detector was 260 °C and the
split ratio was 30:1. Nitrogen was the carrier gas, at a ﬂow rate of
0.8 mL/min.
2.6. Statistical analysis
All analysis of human milk samples was carried out in triplicate. The
results were expressed as means ± standard deviations (SD). The data
were ﬁrstly checked for normality, and then were subjected to one-way
analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey ’s test. The data analysis all use
the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (Version 20.0, Spss Inc.,
Chicago, USA). Results were considered statistically signi ﬁcant at
p < 0.05.

3. Results
3.1. The total fat contents and the fatty acids composition of TGs in Chinese
human milk
Table 1 revealed the total fat contents and fatty acids composition of
TGs in human milk from Zhengzhou, Wuhan and Harbin. The total fat
contents in Zhengzhou (3.90 ± 1.41%) and Wuhan (3.89 ± 1.66%)
were slightly higher than Harbin (3.29 ± 1.17%), but not observed
signiﬁcant di ﬀerence among three regions. Wuhan human milk
(36.89 ± 1.38%) possessed lower levels of SFA than Zhengzhou
(39.20 ± 1.59%) and Harbin (38.08 ± 1.54%). The levels of SCFA
(C4:0-C6:0) in Wuhan human milk (0.04 ± 0.01%) were also sig-
niﬁcantly lower than Zhengzhou (0.07 ± 0.02%) and Harbin
(0.10 ± 0.03%), because the low levels of butyric acid (C4:0) in
Wuhan (0.03 ± 0.01%). Harbin human milk (0.03 ± 0.01%) pos-
sessed signiﬁcantly higher levels of caproic acid (C6:0) than Zhengzhou
(0.01 ± 0.00%) and Wuhan (0.01 ± 0.00%). Zhengzhou human milk
(6.36 ± 1.46%) contained signi ﬁcantly higher levels of MCFA (C8:0-
C12:0) than Wuhan (4.31 ± 0.77%) and Harbin (4.04 ± 0.17%),
which resulted from highest levels of caprylic acid (C8:0,
0.05 ± 0.02%), capric acid (C10:0, 1.12 ± 0.29%) and lauric acid
(C12:0, 5.18 ± 1.14%) in Zhengzhou. The contents of LCSFA (C14:0-
C22:0, 32.53 –33.94%) were not observed statistical di ﬀerence among
three regions (p > 0.05). Harbin human milk possessed lowest levels
of myristic acid (C14:0, 3.51 ± 0.33%) and highest levels of palmitic
acid (C16:0, 22.53 ± 0.52%). The contents of stearic acid (C18:0,
5.42–6.59%) had no signi ﬁcant diﬀerences in three regions (p > 0.05).
Harbin (34.61 ± 0.45%) human milk were observed higher levels
of MUFA than Zhengzhou (33.56 ± 0.37%) and Wuhan
(32.77 ± 1.18%). The contents of oleic acid (C18:1) in three regions
were 30.28 –31.92% and no signi ﬁcant di ﬀerences observed
(p > 0.05). The PUFA contents in Wuhan (30.34 ± 0.33%) human
milk were signi ﬁcantly higher than Zhengzhou (27.24 ± 1.22%) and
Harbin (27.31 ± 1.16%), mainly because Wuhan human milk pos-
sessed relative high levels of linoleic acid (C18:2, 25.92 ± 1.10%).
Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, 18:3n-3) was the most abundant omega-3
family essential fatty acids, the contents of which in Harbin human milk
(1.95 ± 0.16%) were higher than Zhengzhou (1.47 ± 0.15%) and

tional fatty acids composition was calculated ( Table 3). The results

SFA (Table 2 and Fig. S1a–c), the sn-2
intrapositional contents of which
were 69.67 –72.36%. Also, the sn-2 interpositional levels of SFA were

4. Discussion
Chinese have developed traditional dietary habits through their
long history and also formed a rich and diverse food culture. Resulted in
rich food culture, regional di ﬀerences caused regional dietary pre-
ferences, playing an important role in food intake, which was also
evident in maternal diet ( Manli et al., 2019 ). The three regions in our
study possessed di ﬀerent dietary preferences. Zhengzhou located in the
Yellow River drainage areas, and prefer pasta food; Wuhan located in
the Yangtze River drainage areas, and with high intake of fresh-water
food; and Harbin located in Northeast China, where belongs to the mid-
temperate continental monsoon climate, and with rice as staple food
(Fig. 1). It was reported that the dietary pattern in Zhengzhou is
characterized by high intake of carbohydrate ( Manli et al., 2019 ),
which can endogenously synthesize MCFA in body ( Gao et al., 2018 ).
Therefore, the relative high levels of MCFA ( Table 1) in Zhengzhou
human milk may be explained by high carbohydrate intake in
Zhengzhou. The levels of LCSFA, especially palmitic acid, were mainly
linked to the intake of meat and dairy products in countries that not
unusual to consume coconut or palm oils ( Barreiro, Diaz-Bao, Cepeda,
Regal, & Fente, 2018). LCSFA were not observed signi ﬁcant diﬀerences
in our study ( Table 1). This phenomenon may be caused by the in-
creased consumption of animal-based food and milk and dairy products
in di ﬀerent regions, with rapid economic growth in China ( Huang,
Wang, & Tian, 2016). While the contents of palmitic acid in Chinese
human milk (21.16 –22.53%, Table 1) were lower than Nigeria (25%),
coastal Iran (26%) and Italian (about 30%) ( Qi et al., 2018 ), where
consumed high levels of cheese (parmesan), meat and butter, and olive
oil (Barreiro et al., 2018). The contents of oleic acid, the most abundant
MUFA, in three regions had no signi ﬁcant di ﬀerences (30.28 –31.92%).
And the contents of oleic acid in Chinese human milk were lower than
the European countries, such as Italy (39.7 –40.8%), Sweden (41.40%),
Spanish (33.62 –38.39%), UK(33.28%) and Croatia (39.63%) ( Barreiro
et al., 2018 ). This phenomenon mainly related to the intake of olive oil
(containing 63.3% oleic acid) by mothers who live in European coun-
tries, for example the Mediterranean diet in Spanish, Italy, Sweden and
Croatia. Other vegetable oil (like peanut oil and rapeseed oil), nuts,
meat and cheese were also the important source of oleic acid ( Barreiro
et al., 2018; Orsavova, Misurcova, Ambrozova, Vicha, & Mlcek, 2015 ).
With regard to PUFA fraction, Wuhan human milk possessed sig-
niﬁcantly higher levels of PUFA than Zhengzhou and Harbin, for the
relative high levels of linoleic acid ( Table 1). It was found that com-
pared to Zhengzhou and Harbin, Wuhan showed a higher intake of
fresh-water food ( Song & Cho, 2017), which may responsible for the
higher levels of linoleic acid in Wuhan human milk. Because Wuhan

(Table 3). It can be found that the fatty acids distributed at three po-
sition of human milk TGs glycerol backbone were not random. The
special fatty acids distribution in human milk were found associated
with many physiological functions of infants. The SCFA and MCFA,
which are mainly esteri ﬁed at sn-3 position of human milk TGs ( Tables
2 and 3 ) can be ﬁrstly hydrolyzed at stomach and directly absorbed by
portal vein and rapidly generated energy for infants ( Billeaud et al.,
2018). And the long-chain fatty acids, especially unsaturated fatty
acids, released by gastric lipase ( sn-3 selectivity) can increase the
binding of colipase-dependent lipase to the milk fat globule, promoting
human milk TG digestion ( Bernback, Blackberg, & Hernell, 1989;
Bourlieu et al., 2014 ). PUFA, especially linoleic acid, were most likely
distributed at sn-3 position of human milk TGs compared with MUFA
and SFA (Fig. S2). On the contrary, LCSFA were rarely distributed at sn-
3 position of human milk TGs, for the sn-3 interpositional levels of
myristic, palmitic and stearic acids not exceed 8% ( Table 3). Therefore,
it can be deduced that the LCSFA esteri ﬁed at sn-3 position may have
bigger harm of infant ’s physiological function than esteri ﬁed at sn-1
position, which need further experimental veri ﬁcation. And PUFA
preferentially esteri ﬁed at sn-3 position in TGs possessed essential
function for fats totally digestion in infants. LCSFA, especially palmitic
acid, mainly esteri ﬁed at sn-2 position had received wide attention.
Because the unique distribution of palmitic acid can improve fat ab-
sorption and reduce Ca excretion ( Bar-Yoseph, Lifshitz, & Cohen, 2013;
Petit, Sandoz, & Garcia-Rodenas, 2017 ). This phenomenon was ex-
plained by the sn-1,3 positions selectivity of pancreatic lipase, because
2-monoglycerides does not form calcium soaps and can be absorbed by
infants
(Lo’pez-Lo’pez et al., 2001; Petit et al., 2017 ). Compared with
LCSFA, MUFA and PUFA more likely esteri ﬁed at sn-1 and sn-3 position
(Table 3), which seems consistence with this theory. It also should be
noted that the distribution of stearic acid was di ﬀerent with palmitic
acid, for the sn-1 interpositional levels over 80% and sn-2 interposi-
tional levels not exceed 15%, the physiological function of which
cannot be explained by nowadays theory. So, in infants, the physiolo-
gical functions mechanism of speci ﬁc fatty acids distribution in human
milk, especially sn-1 and sn-3 position preference esteri ﬁcation, need
further research.
5. Conclusion
There are di ﬀerences between the characteristics of Chinese diet
culture and the countries currently reported, and there are di ﬀerences
in di ﬀerent regions of China's vast territory and abundant resources.
These di ﬀerences a ﬀect the composition of breast milk. The total and
intrapositional fatty acids composition were a ﬀected by di ﬀerent re-
gions, for relative high levels of MCFA in Zhengzhou, relative high
contents of SCFA and MUFA in Harbin and relative high values of PUFA
in Wuhan, which caused mainly by the di ﬀerent dietary habit. The high
levels of linoleic acid in Chinese human milk were the main di ﬀerence
among China and other countries. The preference esteri ﬁcation of fatty
acids in human milk was hardly in ﬂuenced by di ﬀerent regions, but
aﬀected by the number of carbon and double bone. SCFA and MCFA
were mainly esteriﬁed at sn-3 position of human milk TGs. While LCSFA
were mainly esteri ﬁed at sn-2 position and rarely distributed at sn-3
position. MUFA and PUFA mainly distributed at sn-1 and sn-3 position.
The preference esteri ﬁcation of MUFA in sn-1 and sn-3 positions were
similar.
PUFA were preferentially esteri ﬁed at sn-3 position than sn-1
position. The data in this study was not only an important guidance for
balance maternal dietary pattern but was conductive for infant for-
mulas design, especially in the levels of stereo-distribution of fatty
acids.
